translations.page04_model_comparison.target_feature_e:
**1. Target definition**

- The `salary` distribution is **right-skewed**, so we model `target = log1p(salary)` to shrink the long tail and stabilise residual variance.
- When reporting metrics (MAE, RMSE, MedAE) in USD, predictions are mapped back to the original scale with `expm1(...)` for direct comparison with real salaries.

**2. Scaling**

- Scaling (StandardScaler / RobustScaler) is **fit only on the training fold** and then applied to validation & test — this prevents **data leakage** from the evaluation sets.
- Tree-based models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) do not require scaling; for Linear / Ridge Regression scaling keeps L2 regularization fair across features.

**3. 5-Fold split & Train – Validation – Test**

- **295 records (~20%) are held out as the Test set** (out-of-sample) and used **only once** at the end to evaluate the selected model.
- The remaining ~80% is split into **5 chronological folds** (sliding window). In each round 4 folds train and 1 fold validates.
- The **validation set (used repeatedly across 5 folds)** drives:
    1. Comparing the 5 candidate models;
    2. Computing **CV MAE / RMSE / R² / MedAE**;
    3. Choosing a **model family** (Random Forest is picked here);
    4. **Hyperparameter tuning**;
    5. Running **ablation / robustness analysis**.
- The test set **does not** participate in any of the steps above — this guarantees an unbiased final estimate.
translations.page04_model_comparison.models_roster_ti: The five candidate models — why this lineup?
translations.page04_model_comparison.models_roster_bo:
The 5 candidates are designed to span the full spectrum **naive baseline → linear → regularized linear → bagging trees → boosting trees**, so any winner beats more than just a straw-man model.

| # | Model | Role |
|---|-------|------|
| 1 | **Dummy (Median)** | Baseline. Uses **median** instead of mean because median is less affected by the right-skewed salary tail. |
| 2 | **Linear Regression** | Checks a **simple linear** relationship between X and salary. |
| 3 | **Ridge Regression** | Linear + **L2 regularization** — appropriate when encoding produces many features. |
| 4 | **Random Forest** | Bagging trees — captures **interactions** and **non-linear** patterns between job features. |
| 5 | **Gradient Boosting** | Builds trees **sequentially** to correct the residual/error of previous trees. |

**Metrics to inspect when comparing:**

- **Low MAE & RMSE** — note that RMSE is very sensitive to the right-skewed target and can be inflated by large outliers ⇒ **read alongside MAE and MedAE** for a balanced view.
- **High R²** — proportion of target variance explained.
- **Low MedAE** — typical error, robust to outliers.
- **Training time** — compute cost for periodic retraining.
translations.page04_model_comparison.rf_vs_gb_title: Reading the five-model results — RF vs GB
translations.page04_model_comparison.rf_vs_gb_body:
The two tree ensembles **Random Forest** and **Gradient Boosting** land extremely close:

- **RF**: R² = **0.822**
- **GB**: R² = **0.821**
- The gap is only **0.001**.

Where they differ:

- **RF has ~ \$759/job lower MAE** than GB → smaller typical error.
- **GB has lower MAE SD** → more stable across folds.

**Takeaway:** both tree ensembles are strong; the project picks **Random Forest** for downstream tuning because its mean MAE is better and its feature-importance story is easier to interpret.
translations.page04_model_comparison.rf_tuning_body:
After selecting Random Forest during model selection, tuning on the validation folds produces the following optimal configuration:

| Hyperparameter | Value | Meaning |
|----------------|------:|---------|
| `n_estimators` | **200** | More trees make predictions **more stable** (lower variance). |
| `max_depth` | **20** | Each tree may grow up to **20 levels**, enough to capture complex interactions. |
| `min_samples_leaf` | **1** | A leaf may hold as few as **1 record** — trees can learn fine detail. |
| `max_features` | **0.7** | At each split the tree only considers a **random 70% of features**. |

**Why `max_features = 0.7`?**

If every tree always saw all features, a few very strong features such as **`job_category`** would **dominate the splitting process**, making the trees in the forest **too similar** (correlated). Restricting each split to 70% of the features forces trees to explore different partitions → **de-correlate the trees** → the ensemble gets a bigger variance-reduction benefit.
